title: K-fold Cross Validation in R Programming - GeeksforGeeks
content:
K-Fold Cross Validation is a method used to evaluate a machine learning model by splitting the dataset into K equal parts. The model is trained on K-1 parts and tested on the remaining part, repeating this process K times. The final performance is the average of all test results, offering a more reliable and unbiased estimate of the model's effectiveness.

Working of K-Fold Cross Validation

  1. Decide the number of folds, K.
  2. Randomly divide the dataset into K equal parts (folds).
  3. Select the first fold as the test set and use the remaining K-1 folds to train the model.
  4. Test the model on the selected test fold and record the result.
  5. Repeat the process K times, each time using a different fold as the test set.
  6. Calculate the average of all K results to get the final performance score.

Implementation of K-Fold Cross-Validation on Classification

We are applying K-Fold cross-validation to a classification task using the Random Forest algorithm to evaluate model performance by splitting the dataset into multiple training and test sets.

1. Installing Required Packages

We are installing and loading essential packages for building, training and evaluating the Random Forest classification model.

  • randomForest: Used for creating and training the Random Forest model.
  • caret: Provides functions for training machine learning models, cross-validation and evaluation.
  • ISLR: Contains datasets like Smarket for model training.
  • lattice and tidyverse: Used for general data manipulation and visualization.
R 
install.packages("randomForest")
install.packages("caret", dependencies = TRUE)
install.packages("ISLR")
install.packages("lattice")
install.packages("tidyverse")

library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(tidyverse)
library(ISLR)

 2. Loading Libraries and Dataset

We are loading the libraries and the Smarket dataset from ISLR, then removing rows with missing values and dropping the Year column for model training.

  • na.omit(): Removes rows with any missing (NA) values.
  • select(-Year): Drops the Year column from the dataset to ensure it's not included in model training.
R 
data("Smarket")
dataset <- na.omit(Smarket)  
dataset <- dataset %>% select(-Year)

3. Exploring the dataset

We are inspecting the dataset structure and checking the class distribution of the target variable Direction.

  • glimpse(): Gives a concise overview of data structure and types.
  • table(): Counts the number of occurrences in each class of a factor variable.
R 
glimpse(dataset)
table(dataset$Direction)

Output:

4. Training model using 10-fold cross-validation

We are using Random Forest algorithm with 10-fold CV to train the classification model.

  • set.seed(): Ensures reproducibility of results.
  • trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10): Specifies 10-fold cross-validation.
  • train(): Trains the model using the specified algorithm (rf Random Forest).
  • Direction ~ .: Uses all other variables to predict Direction.
R 
set.seed(123)
train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, sampling = "up")

model_rf <- train(
  Direction ~ ., 
  data = dataset,
  method = "rf", 
  trControl = train_control
)

5. Evaluating Model Performance

We are evaluating the model's performance using a confusion matrix, which compares predicted values with actual values of the target variable Direction.

  • print(): Displays the model summary, including performance metrics like accuracy.
R 
print(model)

Implementation the K-fold Technique on Regression

We use regression models to predict continuous values like prices or sales and apply K-Fold cross-validation to check the model’s accuracy and make sure it performs well on different sets of data.

1. Installing Required Packages

We are installing and loading the necessary packages for data manipulation, training models and accessing the dataset.

  • lattice: Provides functions for creating statistical graphics.
  • tidyverse: A collection of R packages for data manipulation and visualization.
  • caret: A package for training machine learning models and performing cross-validation.
  • datarium: A package containing datasets like marketing.
  • install.packages(): Installs specified R packages from CRAN.
  • library(): Loads the installed package for use in the session.
R 
install.packages("lattice")
library(lattice)

library(tidyverse)
library(caret)
install.packages("datarium")  
library(datarium)

data("marketing", package = "datarium")

2. Loading and Inspecting the Dataset

We are loading the dataset and inspecting the first few records to understand the structure and distribution of variables.

  • head(): Displays the first few rows of the dataset for a quick overview of the data.
R 
head(marketing)

Output: 

3. Training the Model with 10-Fold Cross-Validation

We are applying 10-fold cross-validation to train the linear regression model. The number of folds (K=10) is defined in the trainControl() function.

  • set.seed(): Ensures that the results are reproducible by setting a random seed.
  • trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10): Configures the cross-validation method, specifying that 10-fold cross-validation should be used.
  • train(): Trains the model using the specified method (linear regression, method = "lm") and applies cross-validation.
R 
set.seed(125)

train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

model <- train(sales ~ ., data = marketing,
               method = "lm",
               trControl = train_control)

4. Evaluating the Model Performance

We are evaluating the model's performance by printing the results, which include key metrics such as RMSE, R-Squared and MAE.

  • print(): Displays the summary of the trained model, including performance metrics.
R 
print(model)

 Output: 

Advantages of K-fold Cross-Validation

  • Fast computation speed.
  • A very effective method to estimate the prediction error and the accuracy of a model.

Disadvantages of K-fold Cross-Validation

  • A lower value of K leads to a biased model and a higher value of K can lead to variability in the performance metrics of the model. Thus, it is very important to use the correct value of K for the model (generally K = 5 and K = 10 is desirable).
